question_text: A proof attempts to show that \(a^2+b^2=3ab\) has no solution in positive integers. Suppose a solution with least \(a+b\) exists. Which argument validly contradicts that minimality?

Odd-odd pairs give an even left side and odd right side. Mixed-parity pairs give an odd left side and even right side. Hence both variables are even; dividing by 4 yields the smaller positive solution \((a/2,b/2)\).
Testing \((a,b)=(1,1),(1,2),(2,1)\) gives no solution, so a least positive solution cannot exist.

option_explanations.C: Correct: the parity cases force evenness of both variables, and division of the equation by 4 preserves it while strictly reducing the positive integer sum.

worked_solution: Write \(8i=8e^{i(\pi/2+2k\pi)}\). Every cube root has modulus \(8^{1/3}=2\) and argument \(\pi/6+2k\pi/3\). Taking \(k=0,1,2\) gives the three displayed roots; cubing each gives \(8i\).

option_explanations.A: Divides the arguments by 3 but fails to take the cube root of the modulus.
option_explanations.B: Uses the arguments for cube roots of \(-8i\), not \(8i\).
option_explanations.C: Keeps just one root rather than the complete set of three.
option_explanations.D: Correct: root the modulus and include all three argument branches.

domain_restrictions: \(z\in\mathbb C\); radians; \(e^{i\theta}=\cos\theta+i\sin\theta\).
difficulty_rationale: Polar root construction with all branches and the correct rooted modulus.
